extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting manuscripts to biomedical journals; journal editors and peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal requirements for preparing and submitting manuscripts to biomedical journals, including ethical policies (duplicate publication, trial registration), manuscript structure/formatting, and reporting standards for study designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant or duplicate publication policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must make a full statement to the editor about all submissions and previous reports that might be regarded as redundant or duplicate publication of the same or very similar work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify editor if manuscript includes subjects about which authors have published or submitted related reports; refer to and reference any such report and include copies to help editor decide handling. Policy does not preclude submission of a paper rejected by another journal or a complete report following a preliminary report (e.g., abstract/poster). Press reports of scheduled meetings usually are not breaches but additional data/tables/illustrations should not amplify such reports. If redundant/duplicate publication is attempted without notification, expect editorial action (prompt rejection at least); if already published, notice of redundant/duplicate publication may be published with or without the author's explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable secondary publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary publication (deliberate republication in same or another language or country) is justifiable provided specified conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All the following must be met: (1) authors have approval from editors of both journals and the secondary editor must have a copy of the primary version; (2) priority of the primary publication is respected by a publication interval of at least one week unless negotiated otherwise; (3) the secondary paper is intended for a different group of readers (an abbreviated version could suffice); (4) the secondary version faithfully reflects data and interpretations of the primary version; (5) title-page footnote of secondary informs readers it has been published in whole or part and states the primary reference (example wording provided); (6) the title should indicate it is a secondary publication (republication/translation/abridgement). Permission should be free of charge. Note: NLM does not consider translations to be 'republications' for indexing when the original is indexed in MEDLINE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling competing manuscripts from same study (differences in analysis/interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When coworkers disagree on analysis or interpretation, authors should submit a manuscript that clearly presents both versions and explain differences in a cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer and editorial review may help resolve disagreements. If unresolved and the study merits publication, both versions should be published—options include two papers on same study or single paper with two analyses/interpretations. Editor may publish a statement outlining the disagreement and the journal's involvement in attempts to resolve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling competing manuscripts from same study (differences in reported methods/results)
rubrics_metrics.description: If dispute centers on differing opinions of what was actually done or observed, the editor should refuse publication until the disagreement is resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review cannot be expected to resolve such problems. If there are allegations of dishonesty or fraud, editors should inform appropriate authorities and notify authors of intention to report suspected research misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing manuscripts from same database
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts from separate groups analyzing the same data set should be considered separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interpretations are very similar, preference for earlier-received manuscript is reasonable but not necessary. Editorial consideration of multiple submissions may be justified; different analytic approaches may be complementary and equally valid and justify publishing more than one manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence policy (letters to the editor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should provide a mechanism (correspondence section/column) for comments, questions, criticisms, and brief reports unrelated to published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of articles discussed should be given chance to respond (preferably same issue). Correspondence authors should declare competing interests. Published correspondence may be edited for length/grammar/style, or published unedited (e.g., rapid response); journal should declare its practice. Authors should approve editorial changes that alter substance or tone. Editors may sift out irrelevant, uninteresting, or uncogent material, but must allow a range of opinion and not use correspondence to promote the journal's/editor's point of view; screen out discourteous, inaccurate, or libelous statements and avoid ad hominem attacks. Journals may set time limits for responses/debate, decide whether to notify authors when correspondence about their work will appear, and set policies on archiving unedited online correspondence; these policies should be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplements, theme issues, and special series principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplements (externally funded collections of papers) and externally funded theme issues/special series require special principles to avoid bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles include: (1) journal editor must take full responsibility for policies/practices/content of supplements and have complete control of publication decisions; editing by funding organization not permitted; (2) editor retains authority to send supplement manuscripts for external peer review and to reject manuscripts—these conditions should be known to authors and external editors; (3) editor must approve appointment of any external supplement editor and take responsibility for their work; (4) sources of funding for research/publication and products considered should be clearly stated and prominently located (preferably on each page); multi-sponsor funding preferred; (5) advertising in supplements should follow same policies as rest of journal; (6) readers must be able to distinguish editorial pages from supplement pages; (7) editors and supplement editors must not accept personal favors/remuneration from sponsors; (8) secondary publication in supplements should be clearly identified and supplements should avoid redundant/duplicate publication—supplements should not republish research results though republication of guidelines/public-interest material may be appropriate; (9) authorship and conflict-of-interest disclosure principles apply to supplements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publishing minimum site disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites publishing medical/health information should indicate names, credentials, affiliations, and relevant conflicts of interest of editors/authors/contributors, and other key information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sites should provide documentation/attribution of references/sources for content; information about copyright; disclosure of site ownership; disclosure of sponsorship, advertising, and commercial funding; all dates of content posting/updating. Be cautious in linking to other sites (may imply endorsement)—provide explicit message when users leave the journal site; indicate when links are posted for financial considerations. Advertising and promotional messages should not be juxtaposed with editorial content and commercial content should be clearly identifiable. Electronic publishing issues needing policies include archiving, error correction, version control, choice of electronic or print version as journal of record, publication of ancillary material, and electronic-only publication—editors should develop and implement policies on these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policies for journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising must not influence editorial decisions; journals should have formal, explicit written policies for advertising in print and electronic versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must have final authority for approving advertisements and enforcing policy; use independent advertising review bodies where available. Readers should be able to distinguish advertising from editorial material; avoid juxtaposing advertising and editorial content on same products/subjects; discourage interleafing advertising pages within articles. Advertising should not be sold on condition that it will appear in same issue as a particular article. Avoid dominance by one or two advertisers. Do not carry advertisements for products proven seriously harmful to health (e.g., tobacco). Ensure enforcement of existing regulatory/industry advertising standards or develop own. Consider publishing criticisms of advertisements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactions with the general media and embargo principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should balance public interest with accurate reporting and may use embargo systems to coordinate media release with journal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors can foster orderly transmission of medical information by agreement with authors (no publicity while under consideration) and with media (no release before publication) in return for cooperation to prepare accurate stories. Embargo works on honor system; widespread noncompliance would dissolve it. Very little research requires prepublication release except urgent public health matters; in such cases appropriate authorities should decide and be responsible for advance dissemination, and editors should be consulted. Policies limiting prepublication publicity should not apply to media accounts of scientific meetings or meeting abstracts. Researchers presenting at meetings should be discouraged from offering more detail than presented. When article soon to be published, editors should help media prepare accurate reports by providing news releases, answering questions, supplying advance copies, or referring reporters to experts—assistance often contingent on media cooperating with timing. Apply these principles to material released early in electronic versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to register clinical trials
rubrics_metrics.description: ICMJE member journals require registration in a public trials registry as a condition of consideration for publication; trials must register at or before onset of patient enrollment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy applies to trials starting enrollment after July 1, 2005; trials that began prior must be registered by Sept 13, 2005 to be considered. Clinical trial defined as any research project that prospectively assigns human subjects to intervention or comparison groups to study cause-effect between intervention and outcome; studies designed for other purposes (e.g., pharmacokinetics or major toxicity phase I) are exempt. Acceptable registries must be publicly accessible at no charge, open to all prospective registrants, managed by a not-for-profit organization, have a mechanism to ensure validity of registration data, and be electronically searchable. Minimum registry information required: unique identifying number; statement of intervention(s) and comparison(s); statement of study hypothesis; definitions of primary and secondary outcome measures; eligibility criteria; key trial dates (registration date, start date, last follow-up, closure to data entry, date data considered complete); target number of subjects; funding source; and contact information for principal investigator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript structure (IMRAD) and general formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational and experimental articles are usually divided into Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion (IMRAD); long articles may need subheadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IMRAD reflects process of scientific discovery. Other article types (case reports, reviews, editorials) may need different formats. Electronic formats allow supplementary sections; authors should work with editors on electronic publication formats and submit supplementary material for peer review. Double spacing of all manuscript portions (title page, abstract, text, acknowledgments, references, tables, legends) and generous margins facilitate editing; electronic submissions should also be double spaced. Pages should be numbered consecutively beginning with title page so reviewers/editors can refer to specific portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting guidelines for specific study designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are encouraged to consult and follow reporting guidelines relevant to their specific research design (e.g., CONSORT for randomized controlled trials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CONSORT statement provides items to report and a patient flow diagram. Reporting guidelines exist for various study designs and some are available at www.consort-statement.org. Authors should consult the target journal's information for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page required information
rubrics_metrics.description: The title page should carry specified information to aid editors, reviewers, and indexing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: (1) the title of the article—concise but containing information (e.g., study design) for electronic retrieval; (2) authors' names and institutional affiliations (some journals publish degrees); (3) department(s) and institution(s) to which work should be attributed; (4) disclaimers if any; (5) corresponding author contact details (name, mailing address, phone/fax, e-mail) and indicate whether e-mail is to be published and whether corresponding author is guarantor for study integrity; (6) name/address for reprint requests or statement reprints unavailable; (7) source(s) of support (grants, equipment, drugs); (8) running head (short running head ≤40 characters if requested); (9) word counts for text only (exclude abstract, acknowledgments, figure legends, references) and a separate abstract word count; (10) number of figures and tables. Word counts help editors/reviewers assess fit to journal limits and whether information warrants space; figures/tables counts let staff know if attachments were included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest notification page
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on potential conflicts of interest should be part of the manuscript on a separate page immediately following the title page (placement may vary by journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including conflicts on a separate page prevents overlooking or misplacing disclosures. Individual journals may differ in where they ask authors to provide this information and some journals do not send conflict information to reviewers. See Section II.D for conflicts policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract and keywords requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract should provide context/background, study purposes, basic procedures, main findings (with specific effect sizes and statistical significance if possible), and principal conclusions; keywords may be requested after abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract should emphasize new and important aspects and reflect article accurately—many abstracts disagree with text. Structured abstract formats vary by journal; authors should prepare abstracts in format specified by chosen journal. Some journals request 3–10 key words or short phrases (use MeSH terms if suitable) to assist indexing; if suitable MeSH terms unavailable, present terms may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction content guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context/background for the study (nature and significance of problem) and state the specific purpose, research objective, or hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research objective often clearer when stated as a question. Make main and secondary objectives clear and describe any pre-specified subgroup analyses. Give only strictly pertinent references and do not include data or conclusions from the work being reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: general principle about content timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods section should include only information that was available at time the plan or protocol for the study was written; information obtained during the study belongs in Results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep Methods limited to pre-specified planning information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and description of participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe selection of observational or experimental participants clearly, including eligibility and exclusion criteria and description of source population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain use of variables such as age and sex when they are included (e.g., why only certain ages included or why women were excluded). Define and justify race/ethnicity variables and how measured. Guiding principle is clarity about how and why a study was done in a particular way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical information (methods/apparatus/drugs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify methods, apparatus (with manufacturer's name/address), and procedures in sufficient detail to allow reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give references to established methods including statistical methods; provide references/brief descriptions for methods not well known; describe new/substantially modified methods, give reasons for using them and evaluate limitations. Identify precisely all drugs and chemicals including generic names, doses, and routes of administration. For review manuscripts include a section describing methods used for locating, selecting, extracting, and synthesizing data and summarize these methods in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe statistical methods with enough detail to enable a knowledgeable reader with access to original data to verify reported results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify findings and present with indicators of measurement error/uncertainty (e.g., confidence intervals) when possible. Avoid relying solely on P values; reference standard works for design/statistical methods with pages stated where possible. Define statistical terms, abbreviations, and most symbols. Specify computer software used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Present results in logical sequence in text, tables, and illustrations, giving main findings first and not repeating all table data in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize or summarize important observations; place extra/technical detail in appendix or electronic supplement. When summarizing data give numeric results as absolute numbers as well as derivatives (e.g., percentages) and specify statistical methods used. Restrict tables/figures to those needed to explain argument and assess support; use graphs as alternative to large tables; do not duplicate data in graphs and tables. Avoid non-technical uses of statistical terms (e.g., 'random', 'normal', 'significant', 'correlations', 'sample'). Where appropriate include analyses by variables such as age and sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion content and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize new and important aspects of the study and conclusions that follow from them without repeating data in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For experimental studies, begin by summarizing main findings, explore possible mechanisms or explanations, compare/contrast results with other studies, state study limitations, and explore implications for future research and clinical practice. Link conclusions with study goals but avoid unqualified statements not supported by data. Avoid statements on economic benefits/costs unless appropriate data/analysis provided. Avoid claiming priority or alluding to incomplete work. State new hypotheses when warranted and clearly label them as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: prefer original research and citation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide direct references to original research sources whenever possible and avoid overlong lists of references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review articles can guide readers but do not always reflect original work accurately. Small numbers of references to key original papers often suffice; electronic versions allow adding references and literature searching aids retrieval. Avoid using abstracts as references. Papers accepted but not yet published should be designated 'in press' or 'forthcoming'—obtain written permission and verification of acceptance. Manuscripts submitted but not accepted should be cited as 'unpublished observations' with written permission from source.
